**Six.** And it's a ceiling, not a target.

Here's the reasoning straight from Foundry's operating principles:

- **Founder time is the product.** Past six concurrent retainers, the founder's time per client drops below the threshold that makes Foundry's work distinguishable from a normal growth shop. The depth is the differentiator — volume kills it.
- **The seventh is a "no" you owe the team.** Owen tracks the count. The partners say the no. It's a standing rule, not a case-by-case judgment call.
- **It's tied to three core beliefs:**
  1. *Pricing* — pick six clients a year on purpose
  2. *Channel* — own the loop, not a channel
  3. *Boredom* — refuse work that bores you, even at scale

The practical enforcement: a qualification rubric requires brand AND growth on the same retainer, founder availability of 2 hours/week, and pricing floor cleared. If any of those are missing, it's a no before the conversation goes further.

Worth noting — this belief has been challenged at least twice (Helmsmark and Saltline) when pushback came on taking a seventh. The studio held the line both times. 📈

---

## Plinthworks Paid Spend: Should Leo Open Now?

**Short answer: Not yet — unless the organic gate has cleared.**

---

### The Gates That Apply

**1. Organic-before-paid validation (hard gate)**
Devi Ramanathan stated this explicitly and repeatedly:
> "Let me see organic move first. If the post does not work without spend, the ad will not work either."

This is a studio-enforced rule, not a preference. Plinthworks paid spend does not open until the organic post has run and produced measurable movement. Saltline followed the same discipline — Eliza only approved paid after the organic post cleared a **seven-day revenue cohort**.

**2. Technical claim sign-off (editorial gate)**
Marcus must sign off on every technical claim before the launch post ships. If Leo is opening paid against a launch narrative, the platform team needs to have cleared the copy first. This gate has been enforced on every Plinthworks campaign — it is not optional.

**3. Message validation window (2-week minimum)**
The studio standard: no retainer ships paid creative until the message has been pressure-tested in organic for two weeks. The Plinthworks v2 hero validation window is the top CAC test example in the studio. Opening paid before that window closes introduces spend risk without signal.

**4. Site copy must be validated before ads run**
Leo caught himself on this in Week 10 — he stopped himself from opening Google Ads against unvalidated site copy. That self-stop is now a documented studio standard.

---

### What Leo Needs to Show Before We Spend

| Gate | Status Needed |
|------|--------------|
| Organic post live and running | Confirmed? |
| 7-day organic cohort logged (revenue or engagement move) | Cleared? |
| Marcus sign-off on all technical claims | Confirmed? |
| Site copy validated (not just written) | Confirmed? |
| Message tested for 2+ weeks organically | Cleared? |

---

### Recommendation

Pull Leo into a quick sync. Ask him to confirm which of these gates have actually cleared — not just been started. If the organic window has run and Devi or the brief owner has signed off, the path is open. If not, the studio playbook says wait.

The pattern here is consistent across Plinthworks, Saltline, and even Cloverkin: **the founders who trust Foundry most are the ones who have seen us hold the line on exactly this.** Opening spend early erodes that.

Want me to create a quick gate-check checklist mission, or do you want to bring Leo's status update here first?

Three things have to be true before any brief opens on a retainer:

**1. Three customer calls, minimum**
Maya or Sara has to sit on three customer calls for that retainer first. Not summaries, not transcripts handed over — actual calls. Every line that ships has to be earned by a verbatim quote from one of those sessions. This is non-negotiable across all six retainers.

**2. Founder voice is in the doc verbatim**
The brief doesn't open with a writer typing. It opens with the founder's actual words captured from those calls. Slide two of every kickoff names a positioning trade-off using the founder's language, not ours.

**3. Nico signs the kickoff**
No creative work starts until Nico signs the kickoff. That's the gate. The kickoff sign-off is the formal handoff from intake to production.

---

There's also a pre-retainer qualification layer that gates whether we even get to a brief:

- Brand and growth are on the **same** retainer (never two separate engagements)
- Founder is available **2 hours/week** minimum
- Pricing floor is cleared

If any of those three are missing at the sales stage, the answer is no before a brief is ever on the table.

The pattern that shows up repeatedly in the cortex: retainers that skip the customer-call gate end up re-briefing around week seven. Saltline, Helmsmark, Cloverkin all have signals of this. The three-call rule isn't process overhead — it's the thing that makes the copy distinguishable.

Two things drove it, and one specific failure made it unavoidable.

**The Helmsmark Catalyst**

Weeks 7 and 8 on Helmsmark became the clearest case study in the studio's history. A positioning doc went through five async rounds over 48 to 72 hours per cycle. Joel asked the same CFO-audience question three separate times. Nobody got a definitive answer because nobody was in the room together. It was called the worst approval cycle that quarter.

**The Pattern Behind It**

Async approvals consistently surface the same questions two or three times because no one has to commit to a position in writing the way they do on a live call. "We love it" in Slack without a read-back window breeds false confidence, then a revision request arrives two days later with the same underlying concern that was never actually resolved.

**The Rule That Came Out of It**

Jules locked it in #foundry-leadership and it went into the wiki: no client approval lives in Slack longer than 24 hours. After 24 hours, Riley schedules a call. No exceptions.

The logic is simple: a call forces the question to get answered once, on the record, with everyone present. Async lets ambiguity compound across rounds until the whole cycle collapses.

The Saltline and Almanac near-misses in later weeks confirmed the rule held. Every time someone tried to run approval over Slack, the same pattern re-emerged.

Based on everything in the Brain and company cortex, here is the full picture:

---

## What Has to Be True Before Leo Opens a Paid Account on Any Retainer

**The gate is organic validation first.** Two conditions, both must be met:

### 1. Organic message validation (minimum two weeks)
The studio standard, codified in Week 11 after the Saltline Week 7 near-miss: **no paid creative ships until the message has been pressure-tested in organic for two weeks.** This is not a preference, it's a written standard Leo drafted and the founders signed in partner sync.

The logic behind it came directly from Devi (Plinthworks): *"If the post does not work without spend, the ad will not work either."* Leo tried to move faster on Saltline, ran the quiet-luxury hero for eleven days on roughly $4.2k with flat organic saves, and Devi called it on the Friday call. The account was closed before reopening.

### 2. A winning organic line must be logged
The Saltline paid hold ran through Week 9 specifically because the organic window had not produced a validated line yet. Week 9 produced the winning line. Only then did the paid hold lift. The documentation lives in the Saltline campaign brief.

---

### The underlying principle
*"Paid acquisition before message validation is debt with interest."*

This is the company-level belief that drives the gate. Running paid on an unvalidated message doesn't just waste spend — it compounds the problem, because you're now paying to amplify something that hasn't earned attention organically.

---

### How it shows up across retainers
- **Saltline** — paid held until Week 9 organic window completed. Gate enforced.
- **Plinthworks** — Leo caught himself (Week 10 near-miss) before opening Google Ads on unvalidated site copy. Self-stop referenced in partner sync.
- **Cloverkin** — Marisol vetoed paid acquisition entirely: *"we do not advertise to anyone we cannot see in a clinic."* Geo-capped accordingly.
- **Almanac** — Tomás turned down a paid social pilot outright: *"a paid ad cannot make a stranger trust a cohort."*

The pattern is consistent across every active retainer. When founders push for paid early, Leo holds the gate. When Leo has tried to move early himself, the studio standard or a founder veto has stopped it.

## Friday Status Note Cadence

The operating object that's been reinforced across multiple clients and channels is this:

That's the spine of it. Three gates, same day.

---

### How it runs in practice

**11am — Riley drafts and submits**
Riley owns the first pass. The note goes to the founder (or lead) for review. This isn't a rough outline — it needs to be clean enough to go out if approval comes back fast.

**1pm — Founder review window**
The founder (you or a named lead on the account) reads it and either clears it or flags changes. The 1pm gate protects the 4pm send — if review slips past this, the note is at risk.

**4pm — Client-facing send**
The status note goes to the client. Friday afternoon, not end-of-day Friday. That timing matters: it lands before the weekend, gives the client something to read Sunday night or Monday morning, and signals operational discipline.

The
operating object that's been reinforced across multiple clients

and channels is this:

> **Status note to Riley

by 11am. Founder review by 1pm. Sent by 4pm.**

That's the

spine of it. Three gates, same day.

---

### How it

runs in practice

**11am — Riley drafts and subm

its**
Riley owns the first pass. The note goes to the
founder (or lead) for review. This isn't a rough outline

— it needs to be clean enough to go out if approval comes back fast.

**1pm — Founder

review window**
The founder (you or a named lead on the
account) reads it and either clears it or flags changes. The 1pm gate
protects the 4pm send — if review slips past

this, the note is at risk.

**4pm — Client-facing send**
The status note goes to the client. Friday
afternoon, not end-of-day Friday. That timing matters:
it lands before the weekend, gives the client something to read Sunday

night or Monday morning, and signals operational discipline.

Bottom line:** Status note in by 11, founder eyes
on by 1, client receives by 4. Every Friday, every

what didn't before the week closes.
